newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin says low tax era coming - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin says low tax era coming - newspaper.

text.p: Canada is on the brink of an era of low taxes that will take the sting out of the sharp rise in pension plan rates facing 10 million workers, Finance Minister Paul Martin told a Toronto newspaper on Wednesday.

"I think we are going into an era of lower taxes, very clearly, and the issue is when," Martin told the Globe and Mail in an interview, one day after he presented his fourth deficit-cutting federal budget in parliament.
Martin said that as Canada Pension Plan rates increase over the next six years, Canadians can expect lower tax levels, including lower income taxes, the Globe said Thursday.

In a string of interviews with the editorial boards of several major Canadian newspapers, Martin said he would like to stay on as finance minister if his government succeeds in the next election, expected later this year, to deliver some of the tax breaks he is promising.
Exactly what spending increases or tax cuts Canadians can expect has yet to be decided, Martin told the Ottawa Citizen.

"This process of steadily increasing tax burden that we've seen over the last 15 or 20 years is going to reverse itself. It is certainly the reduction in the personal tax rate that is going to be of prime importance to us," Martin said.

Martin's comments came as parliamentary clamor continued over last week's announced plan to increase CPP rates by 69 percent. Maximum contributions will rise to C$1,635 a year in 2003 from C$945 a year now.
Right-wing opposition in the House of Commons called the CPP overhaul a major tax grab because it will bring in C$10-billion in revenue.

Martin told the Citizen he also predicts a reveral of three decades of gradually increasing unemployment rates, dismissing as no longer valid the Bank of Canada's fears that an unemployment rate of less than eight percent would be inflationary.

Martin reiterated that braod-based tax cuts will have to wait until after the deficit has been cut further. This week's budget calls for a C$19 billion deficit this year, C$17 billion in 1997-98 and C$9 billion in 1998-99.

"I would like to bring in a tax cut as quickly as I can," he said, "but we're not going to bring in a tax cut if it puts in jeopardy our ability to fund health care, our ability to fund education, or ability to really deal with child poverty."
